entry.title: Policy disconnect
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Policy disconnectPolicy disconnect

Ambiguity on satellite communication is creating unease

premium

Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite await security clearances to launch commercial satellite broadband services in India, amid delays in regulatory approvals. (AI-generated image)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 9:46 PM ISTThe recent public spat between stakeholders on approvals related to satellite-broadband service in India points to a systemic problem. It started with Elon Musk, chief executive of Texas-headquartered SpaceX and Tesla, hitting out at potential rivals in India, calling them “oligarchs’’ and blaming them for blocking competition. He specifically insinuated that Reliance Industries Ltd (RIL) might have had a role in delaying the security clearance of Starlink, the satellite-internet company operated by SpaceX. RIL rejected the allegations, saying that it welcomed competition and that Jio Satellite Communications too was waiting for security approval. Bharti Enterprises Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal joined the war of words, stating that his company had been in the queue the longest in starting satellite broadband in India. As for the Union government, Minister of Communications Jyotiraditya Scindia retorted by saying that India did not allow monopolies in any sector.  Bharti Enterprises-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, Starlink and Jio Satellite have all been granted the licence to operate satellite-broadband service in India, but they cannot commercially launch operations without security clearance from the government. Eutelsat OneWeb is reported to have got the Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) licence way back in 2021. Jio Satellite got its licence in 2022, while Starlink was able to make the cut in 2025. The fact that the companies armed with the requisite licence are unable to launch commercial operations is a matter of concern and frustration for businesses. Granting licences and then making businesses wait for the security nod, stretching over years, signifies an adverse regulatory environment. This is especially true when the government wants to intensify its reform trajectory, enabling ease of business and enhancing flow of foreign investments. To help realise the goals of satellite communications, the government departments and agencies must act in sync with one another rather than as individual power centres working in silos. While the licence — GMPCS — came from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), other approvals for satcom are granted by the Department of Space (DoS), Ministry of Home Affairs, and security agencies. In the case of Starlink, it’s been under scrutiny over its alleged role in the Russia-Ukraine war through its communication network.  While the security checks have to be foolproof, the government must provide clarity on the process of approvals and indicate a timeline for starting operations. Some of the satellites engaged for the yet-to-be launched satcom services are fast approaching end of life, having been on hold for so many years. Besides security approvals, there are other deliverables as well. For instance, the Union Cabinet has to give the final go ahead on spectrum pricing. More than a month ago, the Digital Communications Commission (DCC) — the highest decision-making body of the DoT — set satellite-spectrum pricing at 5 per cent of the adjusted gross revenue (AGR) of a telecom company. For services offered to remote and rural areas, there’s a discounted price, at 4 per cent of AGR. This followed a long-drawn dispute over the mode of spectrum allocation for satellite communication. The DCC decision, based on the recommendations of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai), will have to be taken up by the Union Cabinet. India’s satcom journey, expected to benefit low-connectivity areas including rural and hilly regions, should not face any more hurdles.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Satellite telecom sector in India Internet

entry.title: Safety first in road contracts
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Safety first in road contractsSafety first in road contracts

Penalty regime should be backed by rigorous project appraisal

premium

The government's proposed penalties for road construction defects highlight the need for stricter safety inspections and better engineering standards to prevent fatal accidents. | Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ plan to penalise contractors in engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) for deficiencies in road construction leading to fatal accidents marks a significant drive towards enforcing greater accountability and safety in projects. Contractors will be given an opportunity to rectify the error within 15 days of the first accident, with the option for the government to step in to undertake remedial work at the contractor’s cost if the person does not comply within the deadline. If another accident occurs within a year of the first at the same spot or 500 metres from the original location, contractors will be charged ₹25 lakh for each fatality and ₹10 lakh for each grievous injury. Though this punitive framework appears unexceptionable in theory, it amounts to action taken after a tragedy occurs.  The question is whether this move needs to be complemented by a more rigorous project appraisal and inspection regime within the relevant government agencies, to ensure that project design and engineering are optimum in the first place. In a country in which experienced contractors are known to display no mean talent in exploiting contractual weaknesses, zero tolerance should precede a repent-and-pay policy. India has the distinction of having the world’s third-largest road network but also shares with China global leadership in road fatalities. In 2025, India recorded over 183,000 fatalities from over 500,000 accidents, averaging 21 deaths every hour, according to the government data. Poor road design is not the only cause of these. Rash driving and rule breaking too are major contributors, but bad road design does constitute a significant threat. Former Tata Sons chairman Cyrus Mistry’s death in 2022 was partly the result of an engineering flaw on the highway on which he was travelling (though the driver, too, was speeding).  Still, the problem is clearly serious enough for the Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari to flag the issue. Speaking at a road-safety event in August, he identified poorly designed accident-prone stretches or black spots as a major cause of road deaths. He spoke of spending a steep ₹40,000 crore to identify the most vulnerable spots in 100 districts to fix the problem. Though this exercise is good, the question is why it should have been needed. The government uses a mix of models for road construction projects — EPC; the hybrid annuity model, or HAM, part-financed by the government; and the build-operate-transfer or BOT annuity model, in which the government pays the contractor fixed semi-annual amounts.  Typically, payments for road projects are linked to pre-agreed milestones and a portion of the payment is held back for a defect-liability period, which can vary from one to four years. This implies that some level of quality control is baked into contracts. Perhaps the question the government should also be asking is why such a high level of fatality-causing deficiencies happens when a third-party independent engineer or certifier has to sign off on the quality of a road before payment is released. National highways account for over a third of road fatalities. With large highway projects under construction, the need for significantly upgrading the monitoring of engineering and construction quality has become critical. The lives of thousands of Indians depend on it.   Topics : Nitin Gadkari BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Road construction Road safety road accident Road Ministry

entry.title: Institutional stability
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Institutional stabilityInstitutional stability

India needs timely appointments in higher education

premium

Prolonged vacancies in top academic positions raise concerns over faculty recruitment, research and institutional planning

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTSome of India’s premier higher-education institutions are facing a leadership vacuum, with 37 of the 155 Institutions of National Importance (23.9 per cent) operating under interim, acting or in-charge heads, additional-charge arrangements or extensions, according to a recent Hindustan Times analysis. The problem is particularly acute in central universities, where 20 of 48 institutions analysed have an interim leadership or extended tenures. Some vacancies persist despite posts being advertised months or even years earlier. This is more than an administrative inconvenience. Vice-chancellors and directors oversee faculty recruitment, academic programmes, budgets, infrastructure, and research partnerships. Prolonged uncertainty can delay decisions on new courses, the setting up of laboratories, and long-term financial commitments. Interim heads may also be reluctant to undertake major reforms when their authority is temporary. Additional-charge arrangements compound the problem by dividing the attention of senior academics between institutions. Hence, prolonged vacancies can put institutions in “standby mode”, weakening accountability and long-term planning.  The consequences are serious because leadership gaps coincide with wider capacity constraints in higher education. According to an analysis by PRS Legislative Research, 29 per cent of the sanctioned teaching posts in central universities were vacant as of December 2024. For professors, the vacancy rate stood at 56 per cent. These shortages place additional pressure on existing faculty. The appointment process also needs closer scrutiny. The analysis highlights cases in which selection procedures had begun well before the incumbent’s tenure ended, yet successors were not announced in time. Indira Gandhi National Tribal University, for instance, had functioned without a regular vice-chancellor for nearly 21 months, although the post had been advertised in June 2024 and re-advertised in March 2026. Such delays raise questions about administrative efficiency. Disputes over search committees and compliance with selection norms can further erode confidence in the process. Transparent, merit-based appointments are essential to protecting institutional credibility and autonomy.  The government should begin selection at least six months before a vacancy arises. It should establish binding timelines for screening applications, convening search committees and announcing appointments, with periodic public updates on progress. Such reporting would make delays visible and strengthen oversight without giving the government greater control over academic decisions. Committees should have clear selection criteria, independent members and safeguards against arbitrary interference. Interim appointments must be strictly time-bound, with extensions permitted only in exceptional circumstances and accompanied by a clear explanation. Institutions could also have contingency plans to ensure that essential academic and financial decisions continue during transitions. Strengthening leadership continuity and institutional autonomy is essential to improving research, teaching quality, and India’s global competitiveness in higher education. Timely leadership appointments are a basic requirement for that task. Leadership gaps and an inadequate strength of teaching staff, even in India’s premier institutions, could seriously undermine the country’s broader objective of achieving higher sustainable growth and becoming a developed country by 2047.     Topics : higher education vacancies governance Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Improved closing auction
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Improved closing auctionImproved closing auction

Sebi should aim to increase participation

premium

Securities and Exchange Board of India | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:13 PM ISTIt has been 10 weeks since the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) changed the way the stock markets end their trading day. It introduced the closing auction session (CAS) on August 3, with the idea of giving one efficient price for index funds, large institutional investors, and derivatives traders. But, instead, it led to problems — especially for derivatives traders, who decided to stay out of the market because of the unpredictability and volatility during the end session. A new circular dated October 15 addresses the issues and is in the right direction. It has delinked derivatives from the CAS close. The notional average daily derivatives turnover is more than 200 times that in cash. Retail investors account for about 40 per cent of the turnover in index options. The CAS was putting all these traders out of the system. The problems should be fixed in December.  The issue started when the indicative equilibrium prices in the CAS system fluctuated wildly as algo traders entered and cancelled orders, which led to volatility. The CAS settlement price is directly tied to expiring derivatives contracts, where traders had limited visibility of how the market would move. Thus, most derivatives traders and domestic funds stayed away from the market during the auction window. The bigger issue was that cash trading stopped at 3.15 pm while derivatives traded till 3.40 pm. The final value for the benchmark indices that came after the CAS was many a time far away from the closing price at 3.15 pm. Likewise for stocks that are part of the derivatives, or futures & options (F&O), segment.  The volumes handled in the auction are about 1 per cent of the daily cash turnover. The auction filled well on days when indices were rebalanced. For example, on the day of MSCI rebalance there were many buyers and sellers in the auction session and volumes were at 22 per cent of the entire trading day. But in normal days it lacked participants and sufficient volumes. In comparison, on the New York Stock Exchange, the CAS handles 12.43 per cent of daily volumes, and the same is 10 per cent for the Nasdaq. In such markets, it is hard for any single player to move the closing price because the CAS accounts for more than 10 per cent of the volumes. In India, the volumes are only 1 per cent and a small player can move stocks and thereby the index in the auction session and make money out of derivatives trades.  The new circular addresses most of these issues. From December 7, the expiry session goes back to the previous 25-year-old system of volume weighted average price (VWAP) while the daily closing price of underlying stocks will continue to be determined via CAS. Expiring index derivatives will stop trading at 3.30 pm or the same time as the cash markets. The auction will happen afterwards (3.30-3.40 pm) but stock derivatives will continue to trade until 3.45 pm.  This is a return to the old system but the auction stays and sets the official closing prices. But the link between derivatives and VWAP is restored. However, Sebi is yet to address how to bring in more passive funds to participate, improve the securities lending and borrowing mechanism (SLBM) or short selling, or separate auction order types that exist in the developed markets. A working stock-lending and short-selling market would let traders sell borrowed shares in an auction where buyers are bigger in numbers, narrowing the imbalances at the close. Thus, there is more to be done. Most importantly, fix stock lending and deepen the auction pool.     Topics : SEBI Indian stock market derivatives trading Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Sustaining progress
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Sustaining progressSustaining progress

India needs to create jobs to further reduce poverty

premium

India's poverty rate fell to 16.1% in 2023 from 57.7% in 2011, according to the World Bank, but creating better-paying jobs remains crucial to sustaining progress.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe World Bank’s October 2026 “Poverty and Equity Brief” showed that the share of Indians living below the lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.20 a day (2021 purchasing power parity) fell from 57.7 per cent in 2011 to 16.1 per cent in 2023, lifting 496 million people above this threshold. Extreme poverty, measured at $3 a day, declined to 2.6 per cent. The poverty rate at the $4.20 threshold is projected to fall further, from 14.2 per cent in 2026 to 12.1 per cent in 2028. However, nearly 80 per cent of Indians remained below the upper-middle-income poverty line of $8.30 a day in 2023. The challenge is to move above the upper threshold as quickly as possible.  Between 2017 and 2023, an additional 134 million received employment, with the increase being nearly twice the expansion of the working-age population. Yet the real earnings remained broadly unchanged, reflecting the concentration of new jobs in relatively low-productivity activities. The median earnings among the top 10 per cent of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10 per cent in 2023. The rise in youth unemployment from 14.6 per cent in the first quarter of FY26 to 15.9 per cent in the corresponding quarter of FY27 is another warning. All this needs to change. Further reduction in the poverty level and an increase in income levels in general can happen only through rapid expansion in employment opportunities.  The structure of employment in the country will be central to this effort. Agriculture accounted for 43 per cent of employment in 2025, while manufacturing’s share was only 12.1 per cent, according to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). This underscores the need to accelerate the shift towards more productive, better-paying non-farm jobs. Labour-intensive manufacturing, including textiles, apparel, footwear, food processing and electronics assembly, can absorb workers moving out of agriculture. Better infrastructure, industry-relevant skilling, easier access to credit, and predictable regulation can help firms expand and hire. Women’s participation is equally important. Although the female labour-force participation rate among those aged 15 and above was 40 per cent in 2025, as against 33.9 per cent in 2022, the urban rate remained much lower, at 27.7 per cent. The same rate among females in countries such as China and the United States is well over 50 per cent. Expanding women’s access to paid employment will require addressing barriers such as inadequate childcare facilities and unsafe transport, alongside more flexible work arrangements. An International Labour Organization study covering 82 countries estimated that every dollar invested in closing childcare gaps could generate $3.76 in global gross domestic product by 2035.  The geographical concentration of poverty makes state-level action crucial. Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal account for about 57 per cent of India’s poor population, according to the World Bank. Rural poverty, at 19.3 per cent, remains considerably higher than urban poverty, which is at 8.6 per cent. States with high poverty levels must compete to attract investment and generate stable, better-paying jobs. The Union government must focus more on these states to ensure equitable growth in the country.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Job creation in india Poverty in India World Bank report Poverty index

entry.title: Dropping barriers
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Dropping barriersDropping barriers

New Delhi must find ways to prise open China's markets

premium

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has flagged China's non-tariff barriers as a major obstacle to Indian exports, calling attention to the widening bilateral trade deficit.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 9:37 PM ISTSpeaking on the sidelines of the autumn meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok recently, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman highlighted concerns about India’s “exponentially growing” trade deficit with China. The minister pointed out that the problem in this case was not high tariffs but non-tariff barriers, which limited Indian companies’ market access in China. Phytosanitary rules, for example — safety regulations of various kinds — limited imports into China of Indian generic drugs, bovine products, and vegetables. For these sectors, among others, missing out on the large and growing Chinese market is a major problem. Meanwhile, Indian imports of Chinese goods, particularly in electronics, continue to grow at a rapid pace.  Ms Sitharaman’s statement has highlighted a problem that Indian trade policy may not currently be set up to address. India has entered into several free-trade agreements (FTAs) — and the one with New Zealand, for example, is coming into force today. These are important steps, in that they open up access to several vital markets, including the European Union and the United Kingdom. But Indian producers also need to expand their access to other countries, including emerging markets. China’s unwillingness to drop its non-tariff barriers is a major impediment in that effort.  To be sure, too much energy has been diverted over the past 18 months in dealing with the fallout of United States President Donald Trump’s attempt to derail global trade. In trying to minimise the effects of Mr Trump’s volatility on US-India trade, the government has sent conflicting signals on the progress of a bilateral deal with the US. It is unclear if talks are “plateauing”, as Ms Sitharaman has said, or if they are poised for a breakthrough, as some of her colleagues in the Cabinet have implied. But either way, the government cannot allow US-India relations to be its sole focus. The larger questions — such as reforming the multilateral trading system and ensuring that China plays a more responsible role within it — must also be made a priority.  Over the past year or so, India has attempted to reset its relations with China away from the lows plumbed after the clashes on the Line of Actual Control in mid-2020. Partly this was to ensure that Beijing placed no impediments in the way of the development of India’s high-end mobile-phone industry, which is dependent on supply chains that run through the mainland. This is also, as it happens, why concerns about increasing imports from China in the past couple of years should not be overstressed. If those imports are of intermediate inputs, to which value is added in Indian factories before being sold domestically or re-exported, then it is not necessarily a negative. The focus should, therefore, not be on the deficit or the scale of imports, but the failure to scale up exports to China. The finance minister is to be commended for making this point. It should be followed up by a comprehensive strategy that centres market access in New Delhi’s discussions with Beijing. It should be made clear that normalising the relationship will be dependent upon the Chinese leadership’s own choices about goods. It is not enough to drop tariffs. A broader acceptance that other non-tariff barriers must be lowered, alongside a step-by-step plan to accomplish that, should be a priority for India’s engagement with its northern neighbour.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment India China relations India china trade

Today's editorials and columns examine Sebi's revised closing auction framework, leadership vacancies in higher education, PSU disinvestment, insolvency delays and a book exploring Delhi's history.

Illustration: Binay SInha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. Sebi’s revised closing auction rules address the volatility and unpredictability that followed the introduction of the closing auction session in August, particularly for derivatives traders. The new framework, effective December 7, restores the volume-weighted average price method for expiry-day settlements and aligns the trading cutoff for expiring index derivatives with cash markets. Our first editorial notes that India’s auction volumes remain around 1 per cent of daily cash turnover, making closing prices vulnerable to manipulation, unlike in the US. While the changes restore a crucial link between cash and derivatives markets, Sebi must deepen auction participation, strengthen stock lending and borrowing, and improve short-selling mechanisms. Nearly a quarter of India’s 155 Institutions of National Importance operate without permanent leadership, with vacancies and interim arrangements disrupting decision-making, academic planning and research partnerships. Today's second editorial warns that these gaps compound existing faculty shortages, with 29 per cent of sanctioned teaching posts in central universities vacant as of December 2024, rising to 56 per cent at professor level. Delays persist even when selection processes begin well before incumbents’ tenures end, raising concerns about administrative efficiency and institutional autonomy. The government should initiate appointments six months before vacancies arise, enforce transparent timelines, limit interim arrangements and strengthen independent, merit-based selection to safeguard higher education and India’s development ambitions. A K Bhattacharya examines the Narendra Modi-led government’s renewed disinvestment drive, led by the recently-approved IDBI Bank sale, against a disappointing record of strategic privatisation. Four privatisations since 2021 have yielded just Rs 2,818.73 crore, while minority stake sales have accounted for most disinvestment receipts. The government’s growing reliance on PSU dividends and increased equity infusions and loans has further complicated the picture. With fresh listings planned, Bhattacharya calls for transparent reporting of disinvestment and asset monetisation receipts, alongside closer scrutiny of government investment in PSUs. The objective should be stronger returns from public assets without compromising overall capital expenditure. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code’s impact extends beyond resolving distressed firms, argue Aaraadhya Srivastava, Pratibha Kumari and Jithin P. Faster resolutions and higher recoveries initially strengthened lenders’ confidence, improving credit availability and costs. Research shows distressed firms took greater risks while improving operating performance, while import-dependent firms with more pledgeable assets increased capital-goods imports by about 31 per cent relative to comparable peers. However, rising resolution times threaten the framework’s credibility. With restructuring taking an average 1,026 days and liquidation 1,378 days in April-June 2026, the authors contend that timely recovery is essential to sustaining lending, investment and financial stability. Veenu Sandhu reviews John Zubrzycki’s The Shortest History of Delhi, a compact yet richly layered account of a city shaped by successive empires, cultural upheavals and competing visions. Tracing Delhi from its legendary association with Indraprastha through the Sultanate, Mughal and British periods, Zubrzycki blends historical evidence with vivid portraits of rulers, chroniclers and ordinary inhabitants. The review highlights his account of Partition as pivotal to the city’s modern identity, while praising the maps, photographs and informative sections. The book also critiques Delhi’s chaotic expansion, crumbling infrastructure and Central Vista redevelopment, portraying the capital as an unfinished, constantly contested work in progress.

entry.title: Best of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished away
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished awayBest of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished away

Today's editorials and columns examine the trade-offs shaping India's economic policies, from China trade and poverty reduction to rupee management and the hidden costs of clean energy

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTPolicy choices rarely come without a bill. Opening markets can increase opportunity but also exposure. Reducing poverty may leave the hardest pockets of deprivation behind. Supporting one macroeconomic objective can make another harder to achieve. Defending a currency may buy stability while creating distortions elsewhere. Even clean energy carries environmental and geopolitical costs. The difficult part of policymaking is not finding benefits; it is deciding which costs are worth bearing, who should bear them, and how they can be contained. Our first editorial today, “Dropping barriers”, looks at India’s economic engagement with China. New Delhi has reason to seek better access to Chinese markets and press Beijing to dismantle tariff and non-tariff barriers that disadvantage Indian exporters. Greater access could help narrow the trade imbalance and create opportunities for Indian firms. But closer engagement cannot ignore strategic vulnerability or the competitive pressure created by China’s industrial strength. India must therefore pursue market access without allowing economic dependence to deepen. Openness can create gains, but only if it is accompanied by stronger domestic competitiveness and a clear-eyed assessment of risk. The second editorial, “Sustaining progress”, turns to poverty reduction. World Bank estimates suggest India has made significant progress, but aggregate improvement can obscure those who remain difficult to reach. Poverty is increasingly concentrated in certain states, regions and social groups, while employment quality and income security remain critical. The next stage is harder than the last. Sustaining the gains will require more jobs, better targeting and sharper attention to areas that have not benefited equally from growth. Ananth Narayan’s column, “Confronting economic trade-offs”, makes the theme more explicit. Monetary and financial policy involves objectives that can pull in different directions. Interest rates, liquidity, inflation, the exchange rate, fiscal conditions and capital flows cannot all be optimised independently. A measure that eases one pressure can intensify another. The challenge for policymakers is not to eliminate trade-offs, which is impossible, but to acknowledge them, rank priorities and communicate those choices clearly. Rajeswari Sengupta’s column, “RBI’s rupee fix: What is it solving?”, asks whether recent efforts to support the rupee are aimed at the right problem. Measures that ease immediate pressure on the currency may provide temporary stability, but they cannot substitute for stronger underlying capital flows and external-sector fundamentals. If the diagnosis is wrong, the cure can impose new costs without resolving the original weakness. “Dirty truths behind clean energy”, Prosenjit Datta’s review of Nicolas Niarchos’ The Elements of Power, exposes the trade-offs embedded in the energy transition itself. Batteries, solar equipment and electric vehicles promise lower carbon emissions, but depend on large-scale extraction of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other minerals, creating environmental, social and geopolitical risks of their own. There are few costless choices, these pieces reveal. Good policy begins when the trade-offs are made visible rather than wished away.

entry.title: Best of Business Standard Opinion: What sits outside the frame also exists
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Best of Business Standard Opinion: What sits outside the frame also existsBest of Business Standard Opinion: What sits outside the frame also exists

What makes these risks dangerous is not only their existence, but the ease with which institutions can ignore them when they are difficult to measure, explain or fit into established categories

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand3 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTSome risks are obvious. Others sit outside the frame: a national interest concealed behind universal rules, environmental depletion missing from economic accounts, currency exposure left unhedged, financial risk buried in product structure, or an illness whose cause remains disputed. What makes these risks dangerous is not only their existence, but the ease with which institutions can ignore them when they are difficult to measure, explain or fit into established categories. Our first editorial today, “Waiving double standards”, looks at the US’ sanctions policy towards Russian oil. Washington has repeatedly argued for strict limits on countries buying Russian crude oil, yet it has also made exceptions when its own strategic or economic interests are involved. The editorial argues that this selective application weakens the policy’s credibility. The hidden variable is national interest: what is presented as a universal rule is often shaped by the calculations of the country enforcing it. For India, that makes it important to respond — not only to the stated principle but also to the interests driving it.  The second editorial, “Building natural wealth”, turns to what conventional economic measurement leaves out. GDP can record production and income while missing the depletion of forests, water, minerals and other natural assets. Environmental accounts attempt to correct that blind spot by treating natural resources as part of the country’s wealth. The larger point: if depletion is not measured, it can easily be mistaken for growth. Bringing natural capital into public accounting would allow policymakers to see the economic cost of consuming assets that may take decades, or longer, to restore. Mihir S Sharma’s column, “Let the people hedge”, applies the same idea to forex risk. Indians have genuine exposure to overseas currencies through education, travel, investments and other transactions. Yet policy remains restrictive about allowing individuals to hedge those exposures freely. The risk does not disappear because the hedge is unavailable. It simply remains with the individual. Sharma argues that a more mature forex framework should recognise the exposure people already carry and allow them the tools to manage it. Debashis Basu’s column, “AT-1 bonds: The bigger lessons”, shows how hidden risk can become visible only after damage is done. Additional Tier-I bonds contain loss-absorption features that many investors may not have fully understood. The Yes Bank episode exposed weaknesses in disclosure, suitability and regulation. Complex financial products are not inherently problematic, but risks buried in technical language or sold to unsuitable investors can create a false sense of safety. “The mystery of the ‘Havana Syndrome’”, Nicolas Niarchos’ review of Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados’ The Havana Syndrome, looks at uncertainty itself. Years after American officials reported mysterious illnesses, the evidence around their cause remains contested. The difficulty lies in responding to experiences that are real to those affected while the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. What cannot be easily seen or measured still has consequences, these pieces show. Often, the greater danger lies in pretending that what sits outside the frame does not exist.Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Fragmented rules, missing incentives hold back India's green finance growth
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Fragmented rules, missing incentives hold back India's green finance growthFragmented rules, missing incentives hold back India's green finance growth

A unified green taxonomy, standardised legal documentation, and tangible economic incentives are urgently needed

premium

green finance, India green finance market, green taxonomy, RBI, Sebi, sustainable finance, green bonds, ESG, green deposits, climate finance, green lending, NBFCs, green debt securities, SNG Partners

Rajesh Narain Gupta4 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 11:02 PM ISTThe devastating floods that swept through Nepal in August 2026 did more than displace communities and disrupt cross-border trade. They served as a stark reminder that climate risk is no longer a distant, abstract concern, but a reality at India’s doorstep. Events of this magnitude necessitate a hard look at how we are funding our climate response.  Over the last decade, sustainable finance has moved into the mainstream of global capital markets. Green bonds, green deposits; and environmental, social, and governance (ESG)-labelled loans are now supported by thick layers of regulation and third-party verification. Yet, India’s share of the global green finance market remains an underwhelming one per cent. In stark contrast, the European Union (EU) dominates with a 45 per cent share, having successfully created an ecosystem that attracts robust private capital.  The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued climate-finance directions for banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), while the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) regulates green debt securities. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has also pushed for greater transparency through its business responsibility and sustainability reporting framework. However, the intent is often overshadowed by the implementation, which has unwittingly become a deterrent for market participants.  A key challenge stunting India’s green finance is a fragmented regulatory landscape. Regulators are operating through disparate rules and supervisory expectations rather than a cohesive policy framework. The most glaring gap is the absence of a finalised, statutory national green taxonomy. While the European Union’s taxonomy provides a uniform set of criteria to determine sustainable activities, India continues to rely on interim lists.  This absence of an anchor taxonomy forces issuers to seek bespoke legal opinions on eligibility for every green issue. It also creates a gap in documentation, as definitions linked to an official taxonomy are missing. The regulatory architecture demands extensive upfront disclosures, ongoing post-listing updates, and third-party impact reporting. Without Sebi or RBI-approved model documents or standard loan clauses, drafting these regulatory obligations into transaction documents is time-consuming and inconsistent. For smaller issuers, this multiplies legal review costs and acts as a severe barrier to entry.  To fix this, India needs scaled disclosures. The rules currently apply uniformly to all issuers regardless of size. Exploring a reduced pre-listing and post-listing disclosure regime for smaller issuances could heavily incentivise participation. Standardised template covenants for green financing would also ensure greater efficiency and enable quicker legal sign-offs.  Another major bottleneck is the lack of fiscal or prudential carrots. It is a common misconception that regulatory frameworks inherently offer financial perks for green initiatives. In reality, the RBI has not built prudential concessions into its climate finance directions. There are no relaxations on the cash reserve ratio (CRR) or statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) for green lending.  Green deposits are placed on the exact same commercial footing as ordinary rupee term deposits. Because current regulations expressly forbid a differential interest rate, there is no tangible “greenium” to attract depositors or lower the cost of capital for borrowers. ESG ratings are also not yet a mandatory input into credit decisions for banks in India; a higher ESG rating does not automatically equate to a lower cost of capital. Therefore, the pricing incentive for a borrower with strong environmental credentials currently lives in loan documentation rather than systemic regulation.  Permitting differential interest rates on green deposits would encourage both investors and borrowers to participate in the green debt market. Furthermore, the introduction of dedicated green alternative investment funds (AIFs) under the current Sebi regime would ensure a disciplined approach to the green use of proceeds.  India has successfully laid the foundation for a sustainable finance ecosystem. However, the next leap requires moving away from overlapping regulations towards regulatory harmonisation. A unified green taxonomy, standardised legal documentation, and tangible economic incentives are urgently needed. A well-intentioned regulatory framework without matching financial rewards is like an engine without fuel. If India wants to secure its position in the global green finance landscape, it must ensure the rules actually encourage the market to move. ______________________________________________________________________________________________________  The writer is founder & chairman, SNG Partners, Advocates & Solicitors   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: AT-1 bonds: The bigger lessons
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / AT-1 bonds: The bigger lessonsAT-1 bonds: The bigger lessons

The Supreme Court's ruling on Yes Bank's AT-1 bond write-off raises concerns over RBI oversight, financial product mis-selling and the limitations of disclosure-based regulation.

premium

The Supreme Court's ruling on Yes Bank's ₹8,415 crore AT-1 bond write-off has renewed scrutiny of regulatory oversight, investor protection and the mis-selling of complex financial products.

Debashis Basu5 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:56 PM ISTThe Supreme Court has finally drawn a line under one of the most disturbing episodes in India’s recent banking history. On October 15, it dismissed appeals by Yes Bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and the Union government against the Bombay High Court’s 2023 decision to set aside the writeoff of ₹8,415 crore of Yes Bank’s Additional Tier 1 (AT-1) bonds. The issue before the court was whether the authorities had proceeded lawfully in imposing these losses. The court held that the administrator appointed to run Yes Bank had no authority to extinguish the bonds after the final reconstruction scheme came into force. Beyond these legal technicalities, the AT-1 saga throws up two bigger questions: First, the conduct of the RBI as regulator; and second, the entire regulatory philosophy of “disclosure-based regulation”.  

RBI as a “bystander”

Yes Bank’s AT-1 bonds were actively sold to individuals even though the regulatory framework treated them as sophisticated, high-risk securities. This was not merely a case of investors buying something risky and subsequently complaining when the risk materialised. In April 2021, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), not the RBI, completed its investigation into Yes Bank’s gross mis-selling of AT-1 bonds. The findings were devastating. Customers were told that the bonds were effectively “Super FDs”, offering a 9 per cent-plus return with the appearance of fixed-deposit (FD) safety. In several cases, the term sheet was not supplied, and customers were not given adequate confirmation that they understood the product’s features and risks. Sebi said some customers were persuaded to shift money from fixed deposits to these risky securities.  The Supreme Court has called the conduct of Yes Bank, the RBI, and the administrator “questionable”, and said that putting investors at the receiving end of administrative lapses would be “highly unfair”. It specifically said that tighter scrutiny should have been exercised before individual investors were lured into these securities. The court described the RBI as a “mere bystander” in the whole saga. The data placed before the Supreme Court identified 1,346 retail investors with around ₹679 crore invested in Yes Bank’s AT1 bonds. Of these, 1,311 were the bank’s existing customers, with nearly ₹663 crore invested. Sebi found that Yes Bank had failed to ensure that investors understood the risks. It penalised Yes Bank and its executives for the mis-selling, including a ₹25 crore penalty on the bank and a ₹2 crore penalty on then chief executive officer Rana Kapoor. Despite these startling facts, the RBI continued to defend the writeoff.  

Disclosure-based regulation

 There is an even bigger issue here. When India liberalised its financial sector, it embraced what is called “disclosure-based regulation”. The philosophy is that the regulator will frame the rules, including disclosure requirements; the seller will provide them along with the product; and investors, acting intelligently and rationally, will decide for themselves what is good for them.  This concept owes something to the old principle of caveat emptor, or “buyer beware”, which was common in an unregulated world of commercial transactions. If an investor buys a risky product after being told about the risks, the consequences are supposedly the investor’s responsibility. This sounds reasonable until one looks at how financial regulation actually works. Regulators do not merely ask financial institutions to disclose information. They make extraordinarily detailed rules about products, capital, eligibility, distribution, advertising, risk profiling, suitability, documentation, sales practices, compensation, and reporting. They specify what banks and financial intermediaries can and cannot do. They issue circulars, master directions, frequently asked questions (FAQs), clarifications, and enforcement orders. The regulatory state is anything but laissez-faire, the environment in which caveat emptor made sense.  The regulator is sufficiently interventionist to write detailed rules, but then retreats into a hands-off posture to say that investors must bear the consequences when those rules fail to protect them. This creates an extraordinarily convenient arrangement for private interests. The gains from selling complex financial products are privatised; the consequences of bad sales practices are pushed on to investors; and regulatory failure is discovered only after the damage has been done. Like Yes Bank’s AT-1 bonds, AAA-rated bonds of Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd (IL&FS) had been wrongly sold, while mis-selling life insurance to senior citizens is an everyday affair.  If AT-1 bonds were so complex and risky that the regulatory framework specified the categories of investors to whom they could be offered, why should disclosure to an inappropriate investor cure the problem? There is a fundamental information and power asymmetry between a financial-services company and an ordinary customer. The former employs lawyers, accountants, investment bankers, risk managers, and compliance officers. It designs the product, determines the sales pitch, trains its employees, and controls the information presented to the customer. The individual investor does none of these things. To pretend that the two parties become equal merely because a disclosure document has been handed over is to confuse formal consent with informed consent.  It is time to confront the hypocrisy of “disclosure-based regulation” and move towards outcome-based regulation. This would mean asking whether the product is suitable for the customer; whether the seller has an incentive to mis-sell it; whether the customer has the capacity to understand it; whether the institution is complying with the rules; and whether the regulator is actually watching. Today, the answer to all five questions is effectively: The investor was warned. This should change.
